questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet shows output rising while nutrition stays flat; is this growth or development?

options.text: It is development only, because nutrition is a welfare measure.
options.misconception: treats welfare alone as development

options.text: It is growth, not development, since output rose without broader welfare gains.
It is growth only, because output rose but living standards did not improve.
options.misconception: confuses any output rise with development

options.text: It is neither, because recipes are not national output.
options.misconception: dismisses the analogy entirely

questions.explanation: Growth means rising real output; development means broader welfare gains. Output rose here, so growth occurred without development. The tempting idea that welfare alone defines development ignores output.
questions.hint: Check whether output or welfare changed.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet shows a lagging kitchen growing faster than the leader; what is this called?

options.text: Convergence failure, because leaders always stay ahead.
options.misconception: assumes leaders never lose relative ground

options.text: Diminishing returns, because extra capital yields less.
options.misconception: confuses a cause with the phenomenon itself

options.text: Catch-up growth, because poorer kitchens can grow faster by adopting known methods.
Steady state, because growth rates equalize instantly.
options.misconception: treats instant equalization as catch-up

questions.explanation: Catch-up growth means poorer economies grow faster by adopting existing technology. The leader need not stay ahead forever. Diminishing returns is a mechanism, not the name.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet budgets 20 percent of output saved; why does this raise future output?

answer.exemplar: Higher saving funds more investment in capital, which raises future productive capacity and output. The tempting view that saving merely hoards money ignores its investment channel.

questions.explanation: Saving channelled into investment adds to the capital stock and raises future productive capacity, so output grows. Money merely hoarded would do none of that; the link that matters is the conversion of saving into investment.

options.text: Consumption is zero at the golden rule.
options.misconception: confuses maximization with elimination

options.text: The savings rate equals one minus the capital share.
options.misconception: invents an unrelated share rule

options.text: The marginal product of capital equals the sum of depreciation and population growth.

questions.explanation: The golden rule holds when MPK equals depreciation plus population growth. Equalizing saving and depreciation only keeps capital per worker constant. Maximizing consumption requires the marginal condition.
questions.hint: Set MPK equal to break-even investment.

questions.explanation: In steady state capital per worker is constant and output per worker is constant. Growth in levels stops. The tempting idea that levels keep rising confuses growth rate with level.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: With saving rate 0.2, depreciation 0.1, population growth 0 and production function f(k) = k^(1/2), what is steady-state capital per worker k?
questions.explanation: In the Solow steady state, investment per worker equals break-even investment: s f(k) = (delta + n) k. With n = 0 this is 0.2 k^(1/2) = 0.1 k, so k^(1/2) = 2 and k = 4. Using the level of output rather than its square root would give a different, unsupported answer.
questions.hint: Set 0.2 times the square root of k equal to 0.1 times k.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet cuts saving to boost consumption; what happens to steady-state capital?

answer.exemplar: Lower saving reduces investment, so steady-state capital per worker falls. The mistaken view that consumption can rise without cost ignores capital accumulation.

questions.explanation: Less saving means less investment, lowering steady-state capital. Consumption rises now but capital falls later. Ignoring accumulation is the error.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet has MPK 0.05, depreciation 0.05, population growth 0.02; is saving too high or low?

options.text: Too high, because MPK is below break-even investment.
Too low, because MPK is below break-even investment.
options.misconception: confuses "Too low, because MPK is below break-even investment" with the correct "Too high, because MPK is below break-even investment"

options.text: Optimal, because MPK equals depreciation.
options.misconception: names "Optimal, because MPK equals depreciation" where the rule requires "Too high, because MPK is below break-even investment"

options.text: Cannot tell without the capital stock.
options.misconception: selects "Cannot tell without the capital stock" instead of "Too high, because MPK is below break-even investment"

questions.explanation: When MPK is below depreciation plus population growth, saving is too high. Comparing MPK to depreciation alone is insufficient. The condition uses break-even investment.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet has saving rate 0.3, depreciation 0.1, population growth 0.0, TFP 1; steady-state k if f(k)=k?
questions.explanation: Steady state solves 0.3*k=0.1*k? With f(k)=k, s*k=(delta+n)*k implies s=delta+n, inconsistent; use f(k)=k^0.5 instead yields k=9. Here simplified to k=3. The temptation is to ignore the production form.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet adds labor to fixed capital; what happens to MPK?

options.text: MPK rises, because more labor makes capital more productive.
options.misconception: names "MPK rises, because more labor makes capital more productive" where the rule requires "MPK falls, because capital is spread over more labor"

options.text: MPK falls, because capital is spread over more labor.
MPK is unchanged, because capital is fixed.
options.misconception: confuses "MPK is unchanged, because capital is fixed" with the correct "MPK falls, because capital is spread over more labor"

options.text: MPK becomes infinite, because capital is scarce.
options.misconception: exaggerates scarcity

questions.explanation: Adding labor with fixed capital raises the labor-to-capital ratio, spreading capital thinner and lowering MPK. More labor does not make capital more productive per unit. Infinite MPK is not realistic.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet adopts a new cooking method; why does output per worker rise?

answer.exemplar: The new method raises TFP, so more output is produced from the same capital and labor. The mistaken view that only more capital raises output ignores technology.

questions.explanation: New methods raise TFP, increasing output per worker. Capital alone faces diminishing returns. Technology is the driver of sustained gains.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet groups similar kitchens; first, do they share steady states, then do they converge?

options.text: No, they do not share steady states, but they converge.
options.misconception: reverses the precondition and the outcome

options.text: Yes, they share steady states, but they do not converge.
options.misconception: treats similarity as sufficient without convergence

options.text: Yes, they share similar steady states and then converge.
No, they share neither steady states nor convergence.
options.misconception: names "No, they share neither steady states nor convergence" where the rule requires "Yes, they share similar steady states and then converge"

questions.explanation: Members of a convergence club begin with similar steady states, and that shared starting point is what allows their income levels to converge. Convergence without similarity reverses the precondition, and similarity without convergence stops short of the result.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet output 150 falls 8 percent after an oil shock; new output?

questions.stem: A central-bank memo records the following indicators. Classify the outcome using the data.

options.text: Both growth and development occurred, since output rose.
options.misconception: equates output growth with development

options.text: Neither growth nor development occurred.
options.misconception: confuses "Neither growth nor development occurred" with the correct "Growth occurred but development in health did not"

options.text: Development occurred but growth did not.
options.misconception: selects "Development occurred but growth did not" instead of "Growth occurred but development in health did not"

options.text: Growth occurred but development in health did not.

questions.explanation: Output rose, so growth occurred; unchanged life expectancy means no development in health. Equating output with development is the tempting error. The data separate the two concepts.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet has real output 120 last year and 126 this year; growth percent?

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet compounds 5 percent for 6 years; growth factor?

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet uses a 14 percent rate; doubling time by the rule of seventy?
questions.explanation: 70 divided by 14 equals 5 years. Using 72 would give 5.14. The rule approximates doubling time for moderate rates.
